question: Joe Woodland, co-inventor of the barcode, said the idea struck him on a Miami beach in the late 1940s when he dragged his fingers through the sand while thinking about which communication code?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: While at the beach, Woodland again considered the problem, recalling, from his Boy Scout training, how Morse code dots and dashes are used to send information electronically.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the barcode was a product of computer engineering; in fact its stripes are literally stretched-out Morse code drawn in beach sand.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Woodland drew on Morse code (dots and dashes) when he pulled his fingers through the sand at the beach in Florida circa 1948-49.

explanation: He drew the dots and dashes in the sand, then pulled his fingers downward and saw them become thick and thin lines, which is exactly what a barcode is.

question: Bananas are shipped green and turned yellow on schedule in sealed ripening rooms by pumping in a gas that the fruit also produces naturally. Which gas?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: The room is gassed with ethylene, a naturally occurring gas emanated by ripening fruit, for 24 hours.

extra.why_interesting: Shoppers think yellow bananas simply ripened on the way over; in fact ripening is switched on deliberately, with a gas, to hit a shelf date.
extra.verification_notes: Commercial banana ripening rooms are gassed with ethylene, which the fruit also produces naturally; no contradicting or newer info found (https://theproducenews.com/choosing-right-banana-ripening-cycle).

explanation: Ethylene is the plant hormone that triggers ripening, which is also why a ripe banana in a fruit bowl hurries along the fruit beside it.

question: Crisp bags are puffed up with a gas that is not ordinary air. Which gas is used to keep the crisps from going stale and from being crushed?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: The impact of nitrogen gas flushing on the stability of seasonings: volatile compounds and sensory perception of cheese & onion seasoned potato crisps

extra.why_interesting: The 'half-empty bag' is a running joke; the puff is actually a deliberate protective gas, and most people can reason their way to which one.
extra.verification_notes: Nitrogen flushing is the standard modified-atmosphere gas in crisp bags, displacing oxygen to prevent rancidity and cushioning against crushing; no contradicting or newer information found (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6148464/).

explanation: Nitrogen is cheap and inert, so unlike the oxygen in air it does not turn the frying oil rancid, and the cushion of gas protects the crisps in transit.

question: Fredric Baur, the engineer who designed a famous snack container in the 1960s, asked that some of his ashes be buried inside one. His family honoured the wish in 2008. Which snack?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: Some of Baur's ashes were buried in a Pringles can at his request.

extra.why_interesting: Nobody expects a snack tube to be a burial urn; the player gets there by recalling which snack has a container famous enough to be its designer's pride.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Baur designed the Pringles can and some of his ashes were buried in a Pringles can after his death in 2008.

explanation: Baur was so proud of the stackable crisp tube that his children stopped at a shop on the way to the funeral home to buy the can, debating only which flavour.

question: In 1937 an Oklahoma grocer named Sylvan Goldman invented the shopping trolley by fixing two wire baskets to a wheeled version of which piece of everyday furniture?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: He found a wooden folding chair and put a basket on the seat and wheels on the legs.

extra.why_interesting: The trolley feels like it must always have existed; learning it began as a chair on wheels, and that shoppers initially refused to use it, reframes an invisible object.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Goldman's 1937 cart derived from a wooden folding chair fitted with wheels and baskets, then a frame holding two wire baskets.

explanation: Goldman's carts were based on a folding chair with baskets where the seat would be, and shoppers ignored them until he hired people to push them around the store looking happy.

question: Until 1916 a clerk fetched your groceries from behind a counter. That year Clarence Saunders opened the first self-service grocery store in Memphis, Tennessee, under which oddly animal-themed name?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: Piggly Wiggly was the first self-service grocery store.

extra.why_interesting: Self-service shopping seems too basic to have an inventor, yet it has a date, a city and a deliberately silly name that still trades today.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Clarence Saunders opened the first Piggly Wiggly, the first self-service grocery, in Memphis in 1916; I found no newer development that changes this.

explanation: Saunders patented the self-service format and never properly explained the name, though he reportedly said he chose it so that people would ask exactly that question.

question: Despite its name, an ordinary tin can of beans is almost entirely made of which metal, with only a whisper-thin coating of actual tin?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: Tinplate consists of sheets of steel coated with a thin layer of tin to impede rusting.

extra.why_interesting: The name says tin, and most people have never questioned it; the metal is almost entirely something else.
extra.verification_notes: Tin cans are tinplate, i.e. steel with a very thin tin coating (about 0.4–2.1 μm), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinplate.

explanation: The can is tinplate, a steel sheet with a tin layer thinner than a human hair to stop it rusting, which is also why a magnet sticks to it.

question: True or false: the small letter 'e' printed beside the weight on packaged food across Europe certifies that the quantity inside is exact.
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: the average quantity of product in a batch of prepackages shall not be less than the nominal quantity stated on the label

extra.why_interesting: Most shoppers have seen the little 'e' thousands of times and either ignored it or assumed it promises precision; it promises the opposite.
extra.verification_notes: The ℮ mark means the batch's average content is not below the nominal quantity, with permitted per-pack tolerances, so it does not certify an exact quantity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimated_sign).

explanation: The 'e' is the EU estimated sign, meaning the batch average meets the stated weight while individual packs may fall slightly under within set tolerances.

question: A chocolate bar left too long in a cupboard develops a dusty whitish coating that is often mistaken for mould. What does the confectionery trade call this harmless effect?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: Chocolate that has 'bloomed' is still safe to eat (as it is a non-perishable food due to its sugar content), but may have an unappetizing appearance and surface texture.

extra.why_interesting: Most people throw the bar away thinking it is mould; the trade has a gentle, almost poetic name for a completely safe effect.
extra.verification_notes: Chocolate bloom (fat or sugar bloom) is the standard trade term for the harmless whitish coating, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Fat bloom happens when cocoa butter migrates to the surface and recrystallises, and sugar bloom when moisture dissolves surface sugar; both are safe to eat.

question: Supermarket apples can be almost a year old, because growers keep them in sealed rooms where one gas in the air is cut from its normal 21 percent down to around 1 or 2 percent. Which gas?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: the normal 21% of O2 concentration of the air should be reduced to 1-3% by flushing the storage room with nitrogen gas

extra.why_interesting: Shoppers picture apples arriving from a recent harvest; many were picked a year ago and kept half-asleep in rooms where the air itself has been changed.
extra.verification_notes: Controlled-atmosphere apple storage lowers oxygen from 21% to about 1-3%, consistent with the claimed answer (https://extension.umd.edu/resource/controlled-atmosphere-storage-apples).

explanation: With almost no oxygen the apples barely breathe, so ripening nearly stops, and the rooms are so low in oxygen that workers must not enter them without ventilation.

question: A bag of crisps always looks half empty, but it isn't filled with ordinary air. Which gas is pumped in to keep the crisps crisp and cushioned?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: Manufacturers use modified atmosphere packaging by flushing the pack with nitrogen to push out oxygen before sealing.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the empty space is just air padding a half-filled bag; it is a deliberately chosen gas that keeps the crisps from going stale.
extra.verification_notes: Crisp bags are nitrogen-flushed to displace oxygen and cushion the contents; see the cited source for the packaging process.

explanation: Oxygen would turn the frying oil rancid, so manufacturers flush the bag with nitrogen, which also acts as a protective airbag so the crisps don't arrive as crumbs.

question: In June 1974, a cashier in Troy, Ohio scanned the first barcode ever used at a supermarket checkout. The item cost 67 cents and a pack of it now sits in the Smithsonian. What kind of product was it?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: The first retail scan of a product marked with a Universal Product Code was a 10-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum that cost 67 cents.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the first scanned product to be something substantial like milk or cereal; it was a tiny impulse buy pulled from a cashier's basket to prove even small items could carry a barcode.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple sources confirm the first UPC scan on June 26, 1974 at Marsh in Troy, Ohio was a 67-cent 10-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum, now at the Smithsonian (https://www.gs1.org/articles/marsh-holds-place-honor-history-gs1-barcode).

explanation: It was a multipack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit, chosen partly to show that a barcode could fit on something that small.

question: On the egg shelf, some eggs are white and some are brown. What one thing about the hen decides which shell colour she lays?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: The color of an egg is primarily determined by the chicken's genetics, and the breed of hen will usually indicate what egg color will be produced.

extra.why_interesting: Many shoppers believe brown eggs are more natural, organic or healthier, or that the colour comes from feed; in fact it is simply genetics, and the two are nutritionally the same.
extra.verification_notes: Eggshell colour is genetically determined and breed is the standard answer; earlobe colour is only a predictor with exceptions, so no clear error (see https://layinghens.hendrix-genetics.com/en/articles/eggshell-color-eggsplained/).

explanation: It has nothing to do with diet, freshness or farming method, and as a rough guide you can even predict it from the hen's earlobes: white earlobes, white eggs; red earlobes, brown eggs.

question: The Nutri-Score label, which grades a food from a green A down to a red E, now appears on packets across much of Europe. Which country invented it and adopted it first, in 2017?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: adopted by the French Ministry of Health in early 2017.

extra.why_interesting: Because the label is so visible on German and Benelux shelves, players often guess Germany or the EU itself; the country famous for rich food and cheese is the one that invented the nutrition traffic light.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Nutri-Score was developed by Santé Publique France and France was first to adopt it in 2017; later adopters came in 2019-2021.

explanation: It was designed by France's public health agency and launched there in 2017, and Germany, Belgium, Spain and others only adopted it later, so despite the Germanic-looking name it is a French idea.
